description.en: The alternate leg raise with head up combines a crunch hold with alternating leg raises. The head off the floor adds upper ab tension while the legs lift one at a time.

en: Lie on your back with the legs extended.
Place the hands at the temples or behind the head.
Brace the core and lift the head and shoulders off the floor.
Hold the crunch position throughout the set.
Lift one leg up toward the ceiling keeping it straight.
Lower the leg back to just above the floor.
Lift the other leg up.
Continue alternating for the desired number of repetitions per leg.
Trains the upper and lower abs together.
Builds core endurance under continuous tension.
No equipment needed.
Hammers the hip flexors.
Carryover to V ups and hanging leg raises.
Develops total core stability.

description.en: The band bent over lat pulldown is performed by anchoring a band overhead and bending the torso forward at the hips while pulling the band handles down toward the hips. The bent torso position changes the angle of pull and biases the lats. It is a great home lat builder.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead, such as in a doorway.
Stand facing the anchor and grab a handle in each hand.
Step back to add tension to the band.
Hinge forward at the hips with a slight bend in the knees.
Brace your core and keep your back flat.
Start with arms extended overhead toward the anchor.
Pull the handles down toward your hips by driving the elbows down.
Squeeze the lats hard, then return slowly to the start.
Targets the lats
Easy to set up at home
No machine required
Builds back width
Joint-friendly variation
Strong lat builder

description.en: The band high fly uses resistance bands anchored at a high point. By pulling the bands forward and down in a fly motion, you target the upper chest and front delts. The high anchor point creates an angle that emphasizes the upper pec, similar to a high-to-low cable crossover.

en: Anchor resistance bands at a high point on each side.
Stand between the anchors with a band end in each hand.
Step forward to create tension in the bands.
Hold the bands with arms extended out and slightly above shoulder height.
Brace your core and step into a staggered stance for stability.
Pull both bands forward and down in a wide arc toward your hips.
Bring your hands together at hip level in front of your body.
Slowly return to the starting position with control.
Targets upper chest fibers
High-to-low angle similar to cable crossover
Constant band tension through the range
Builds chest size and definition
Useful for home training
Easy to scale by changing band tension

description.en: The band single stiff leg deadlift with single arm row is a combo move that pairs a single leg RDL with a band row. The lifter hinges on one leg, rows the band, and stands back up. It builds the posterior chain, back, and balance in one move.

en: Stand on one leg with a resistance band anchored in front.
Grip the band handle with the opposite hand.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Hinge at the hip and lift the back leg behind you.
Lower the torso toward parallel with the floor.
Row the band handle to the lower ribs at the bottom.
Lower the band and stand back up to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Builds the posterior chain
Trains balance
Combines hinge and row
Strong combo move
Useful functional move
Builds the back

description.en: The band standing twisting crunch is a standing crunch with rotation using a resistance band anchored at chest height. As you crunch your torso forward, you twist toward one side, loading the obliques against the band tension. It is a strong choice for standing oblique training.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height.
Stand sideways to the anchor, gripping the band ends with both hands at your chest.
Step away to create tension.
Brace your abs and stand tall.
Crunch your torso forward and twist away from the anchor.
Bring the band ends across your body toward the far hip.
Squeeze the obliques hard at the bottom of the twist.
Return to the starting position. Complete reps then switch sides.
Loaded standing oblique work
Constant band tension
Builds rotational core strength
No floor work required
Different stimulus than lying twists
Useful for athletic carryover

description.en: The band twisting overhead press combines an overhead press with a torso rotation. Standing on a band with the ends gripped at the shoulders, you press the bands overhead while rotating the torso. The combination trains the shoulders and core in one rotational pattern with strong functional carryover.

en: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the band ends at shoulder height with palms facing forward.
Brace your core hard.
As you press the right band end overhead, rotate your torso to the left.
Drive through your right hip and rotate your trunk through the press.
Lock out the band overhead with torso rotated.
Reverse the motion, lowering the band end and rotating back to center.
Repeat on the other side, alternating.
Trains shoulders and core in one rotational motion
Strong functional carryover
Builds rotational power
Constant band tension through the range
Useful for athletes who need rotational power
Easy to scale by changing band tension

description.en: The barbell block pull, or rack pull from blocks, raises the starting position of the deadlift by setting the plates on stacked blocks or platforms. The shorter range of motion lets you handle more weight than a floor pull, building lockout strength and overloading the upper back, traps, and grip.

en: Stack blocks or platforms on each side of the lifting area to raise the bar.
Set the bar height so the plates rest just below or above your knees, depending on the variation.
Approach the bar in a conventional deadlift stance with feet hip-width apart.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar just outside your legs.
Pull the slack out of the bar, engage your lats, and brace your core.
Drive through your heels to stand up with the bar.
Lock out at the top with hips fully extended and shoulders pulled back.
Lower the bar back to the blocks with control.
Allows heavier loads than full deadlifts
Builds lockout strength
Overloads the upper back, traps, and grip
Reduces stress on the lower back compared to a floor pull
Excellent accessory for competition deadlift
Useful for working through deadlift sticking points

description.en: The barbell front rack split squat holds a barbell in the front rack position while performing stationary split squats. The front-loaded position forces an upright torso, emphasizing the quadriceps and core more than back-loaded variations.

en: Clean or unrack a barbell to the front rack — across your front shoulders, elbows high.
Step one foot forward into a split stance. Feet hip-width apart for balance.
This is your fixed position for the set.
Lower your back knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Keep your torso upright — the front rack demands this.
Drive through your front foot to return to the top of the split stance.
Complete reps, then switch which foot is forward.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 10 reps per leg.
Front rack forces upright torso for quad emphasis
Builds single-leg strength with barbell loading
Develops core anti-flexion strength
Useful for Olympic lifting accessory work
Stationary position allows focused loading
Builds rack position endurance

description.en: The barbell jump squat is a plyometric exercise where you perform a back-loaded squat and explosively jump out of the bottom with the bar across your upper back. The added load increases power demand significantly. Use light loading (typically 20 to 40 percent of squat 1RM) to maintain explosiveness without sacrificing form.

en: Set up a light barbell across your upper traps in a power rack. Use lighter weight than your normal squat.
Step back from the rack. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out.
Brace your core. Sit your hips back and down into a partial-to-parallel squat.
From the bottom, explode upward with maximum effort. Jump off the floor.
Fully extend at the peak of the jump.
Land softly with bent knees. Sit back into the next squat to absorb impact.
Maintain control throughout. The bar must stay tight on your back.
Perform 3 to 6 reps per set with full recovery. This is a power exercise — never train it to failure.
Builds explosive lower-body power
Develops fast-twitch fiber recruitment
Trains the squat pattern under explosive demand
Carries over to vertical jump and sprint performance
Bridge from bodyweight jump squats to weighted plyometrics
Builds functional power for athletes

description.en: The barbell rear delt row is a horizontal pulling exercise where you row a barbell with a wide overhand grip and flared elbows, targeting the rear deltoids and mid-traps rather than the lats. The wide grip and high-elbow path distinguish it from a standard bent-over row and make it one of the most effective barbell exercises for building rear-delt thickness.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Grip a barbell with a wide overhand grip — roughly 1.5 times shoulder-width.
Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees from horizontal.
Let the bar hang at arm’s length. Brace your core and lock in your back angle.
Row the bar up by driving your elbows up and out to the sides — not back toward your hips.
Pull the bar to your upper chest or clavicle area. Your elbows should be at or above shoulder height at the top.
Squeeze your rear delts and mid-traps hard. Pause briefly.
Lower the bar under control. Maintain the same torso angle throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use lighter weight than standard rows — this is a precision exercise.
Targets the rear delts and mid-traps more than standard rows
Wide grip and high elbows shift emphasis away from the lats
Builds rear-delt thickness for balanced shoulders
Improves posture and shoulder health
Allows heavier loading than dumbbell rear delt flies
Excellent accessory for overhead pressing and bench pressing

description.en: The battling ropes outside circle is a battle rope drill where the rope ends move in outward circular patterns. The arms rotate outward to create the circles. It builds the shoulders, rear delts, and rotational core endurance.

en: Grip both battle rope ends with the arms at the sides.
Stand with the feet shoulder width apart facing the anchor.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Begin moving the rope ends in outward circles.
Both arms rotate outward away from each other.
Keep the circles big and continuous.
Maintain a steady pace throughout.
Continue for the working set.
Trains the rear delts
Builds shoulder endurance
Strong conditioning move
Useful for athletes
Burns calories

description.en: The body extension is a full-body standing stretch where you reach both arms straight overhead and arch backward, extending through your entire spine. It opens the front of the body, decompresses the spine, and is excellent for counteracting the rounded posture caused by prolonged sitting.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Reach both arms straight up overhead, palms facing forward or each other.
Engage your core gently. Squeeze your glutes for low-back support.
Lift your chest tall and slowly arch your upper back, reaching your hands back behind you.
Look up gently if comfortable. Keep your neck long.
Lengthen through the entire spine.
Hold for 5 to 15 seconds at the deepest point.
Slowly return to upright. Repeat 3 to 5 times.
Opens the entire front of the body
Decompresses the spine
Counteracts hunched posture from sitting
Stretches the abs, hip flexors, and chest
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible

description.en: The bodyweight lying shoulder external rotation is a shoulder mobility and rehab drill. Lying on the side with the elbow at 90 degrees and rotating the forearm up trains the infraspinatus and teres minor.

en: Lie on your side with the bottom arm under your head for support.
Bend the top elbow to 90 degrees with the upper arm against your side.
The forearm should rest across the abdomen.
Brace the core and keep the upper arm pinned against the body.
Rotate the forearm up by externally rotating the shoulder.
Stop when the forearm is roughly vertical.
Lower the forearm slowly back to the abdomen.
Complete all reps on one side then switch.
Strengthens the rotator cuff muscles.
Improves shoulder health and pre lifting prep.
Trains the often weak external rotators.
No equipment needed.
Excellent shoulder warm up before pressing.
Helps prevent common shoulder injuries.

description.en: The bodyweight single leg KAS glute bridge is a partial range single leg hip thrust variation popularized by Kassem Hanson. The shoulders are elevated and the range is short to bias the top end glute squeeze.

en: Set up with the upper back resting on a bench or step.
Plant one foot flat on the floor and extend the other leg.
Lift the hips up into a single leg bridge.
Brace the core and squeeze the glute on the working side.
Lower the hips just slightly from the top position.
Drive back up to lockout by squeezing the glute hard.
Keep the range short and the tension on the glute.
Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Builds glute strength at the top of hip extension.
Short range bias trains the glute lockout.
No equipment needed beyond a bench.
Carryover to single leg hip thrusts.
Improves single leg hip stability.
Develops glute size and contraction strength.

description.en: The bottle weighted Romanian deadlift uses filled water bottles or jugs as makeshift weights for the classic Romanian deadlift hinge pattern. Holding a heavy bottle in each hand, you hinge at the hips to load the hamstrings and glutes. It is a strong choice for home training when no traditional weights are available.

en: Fill two water bottles or jugs with water or sand for resistance.
Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a bottle in each hand at your thighs.
Pull your shoulders back and brace your core.
Maintain a slight soft bend in the knees.
Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back behind you.
Lower the bottles along the front of your legs while keeping them close.
Continue lowering until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings.
Drive your hips forward to stand back up to the starting position.
Trains the hinge pattern with no traditional weights
Builds posterior chain strength at home
Easy to scale by changing bottle weight
Maximizes hamstring stretch
Develops glute and hamstring strength
Practical for travel or home training

description.en: The bottle weighted side bend uses a filled water bottle as a substitute weight for a side bend. The lifter holds the bottle in one hand and bends sideways. It is a useful home option for training the obliques.

en: Hold a filled water bottle in one hand at the side.
Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Place the other hand on the hip.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Bend sideways toward the bottle hand.
Pause briefly at the bottom.
Drive the obliques to lift the torso back up.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Trains the obliques
No weights needed
Strong home option
Useful core builder
Builds the side abs

description.en: The cable bent over row with bar combines the bent over row pattern with the constant tension of a low cable. The straight bar attachment lets the lifter pull from a wide grip up to the chest. The cable keeps the lats and back loaded through the entire range.

en: Attach a straight bar to a low cable pulley.
Stand facing the machine with feet at shoulder-width.
Hinge at the hips with a flat back and slight knee bend.
Grip the bar with hands wider than shoulder-width.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Row the bar up to your lower chest by driving the elbows back.
Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row.
Lower the bar back down with control.
Constant cable tension
Builds upper back strength
Trains the lats and rhomboids
Strong bent over row variation
Excellent back day move
Adjustable resistance

description.en: The cable lying close press is performed lying on a flat bench between two low cables. Pressing handles together with a close grip targets the triceps and inner chest. The cables provide constant tension that builds tricep size and lockout strength.

en: Set both cable pulleys to the lowest position with single handles.
Position a flat bench between the two cable stations.
Lie back on the bench with handles in each hand.
Hold the handles together over your chest with arms extended, palms facing each other.
Plant your feet flat and brace your core.
Lower the handles to your chest while keeping them close together.
Allow your elbows to tuck close to your sides as you lower.
Press the handles back up by extending the elbows. Squeeze the triceps at the top.
Constant cable tension through the range
Targets triceps with close grip
Builds inner chest as well as triceps
Useful tricep variation for cable users
Strong lockout strength development
Different stimulus than barbell close grip press

description.en: The close grip chin-up is a chin-up variation performed with hands placed close together (roughly shoulder-width or narrower) in an underhand grip. The narrow underhand grip combines maximum bicep involvement with strong lat engagement, making it one of the most effective bodyweight exercises for arm and back development.

en: Reach up and grip a pull-up bar with an underhand (palms-toward-you) grip, hands shoulder-width apart or slightly narrower.
Hang with arms fully extended. Cross your ankles. Brace your core.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position.
Pull your body up by driving your elbows down and back. Lead with your chest.
Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your biceps and lats hard at the top.
Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
This is one of the easier pull-up variations for most people due to bicep involvement.
Maximum bicep involvement of any pull-up variation
Builds the lats, biceps, and brachialis simultaneously
Often easier than wide-grip pull-ups due to bicep contribution
Excellent for arm size and back width
No equipment needed beyond a pull-up bar
Easy to load with weight

description.en: Cocoons lie flat with arms overhead and legs extended, then simultaneously crunch the torso up and tuck the knees in — forming a tight ball (cocoon). It engages both the upper and lower abs through full range in one movement.

en: Lie flat. Arms extended overhead, legs extended.
Simultaneously crunch your torso up and tuck your knees toward your chest.
Wrap your arms around your knees — forming a tight ball.
Extend everything back to flat.
Move with control.
The simultaneous crunch and tuck engages the entire rectus abdominis.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Similar to V-ups but with knee tuck instead of straight legs.
Engages upper and lower abs simultaneously
Full range of motion core exercise
No equipment needed
Builds ab strength through complete range
Easier than V-ups (bent knees)
Develops coordination

description.en: The crunchy frog is a Pilates style core move popularized in P90X. The lifter balances on the tailbone with arms and legs extended, then folds the body into a tight ball with bent knees. The open-and-close pattern hammers the abs and hip flexors hard.

en: Sit on the floor balanced on the tailbone with knees bent.
Lean back slightly with the arms extended out to the sides.
Brace your core hard.
Extend the legs straight out and lean back at the same time.
Open the arms wide as the legs extend.
Pull the knees back into the chest while wrapping the arms around the shins.
Squeeze the abs hard in the tucked position.
Continue the open and close motion with control.
Brutal abs builder
Trains hip flexors
No equipment needed
Strong Pilates move
Builds full core strength
Useful core finisher

description.en: The downward facing dog spine mobility takes a static downward dog and adds gentle spinal movement. The flowing motion mobilizes the entire back while stretching the hamstrings and shoulders.

en: Start in a high plank with hands under shoulders and body straight.
Push the hips up and back into a downward facing dog.
Press the chest toward the thighs and aim heels toward the floor.
From the dog position, round the spine by tucking the tailbone.
Then arch the spine and lift the chest toward the floor.
Continue alternating between rounding and arching the spine.
Keep the arms strong and the hands grounded.
Maintain steady breathing through every movement.
Mobilizes the entire spine through flexion and extension.
Stretches the hamstrings and calves.
Opens the shoulders and chest.
Decompresses the lumbar spine.
Improves overall spinal health.
No equipment needed.

description.en: The dumbbell decline twist fly performs the standard decline dumbbell fly with an added wrist rotation through the rep. As your arms reach full extension at the top of the fly, you rotate your wrists so palms face forward, then reverse the rotation as you lower. The rotation adds rotator cuff work and increases pec contraction.

en: Set a bench to a decline angle and secure your feet on the foot pads.
Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand.
Start with arms extended over your chest, palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Lower the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc.
As you press the dumbbells back up, rotate your wrists so palms face forward at the top.
Squeeze your chest at the top with the rotation completed.
Reverse the rotation as you lower for the next rep.
Adds wrist rotation to decline fly
Increases pec contraction at the top
Trains rotator cuff and external rotation
Builds lower chest size
Different stimulus than standard decline fly
Useful for breaking through chest plateaus

description.en: The dumbbell kneeling Arnold press is performed in a tall kneeling position with both knees on the floor. The kneeling stance removes any leg drive from the press, forcing the shoulders to do all the work. The Arnold press rotation hits all three deltoid heads while the kneeling position challenges core stability.

en: Kneel on a soft surface with both knees on the floor and torso upright.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level with palms facing you.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to lock the hips.
Press the dumbbells up while rotating your wrists outward.
At the top, palms face forward and arms are extended overhead.
Squeeze your shoulders at lockout.
Lower the dumbbells back down while reversing the rotation.
Return to the supinated grip at the shoulder.
Removes leg drive for strict shoulder work
Tall kneeling position challenges core
Hits all three deltoid heads through rotation
Builds shoulder size and definition
Strong glute engagement to maintain posture
Excellent for hypertrophy training

description.en: The dumbbell one arm chest fly on exercise ball is a unilateral chest fly done bridged on a stability ball. Working one side at a time forces the core to resist rotation while the chest does the fly.

en: Sit on a stability ball with a dumbbell in one hand.
Walk the feet out and bridge the upper back onto the ball.
Press the hips up so the torso is parallel to the floor.
Hold the dumbbell over the chest with a slight elbow bend.
Brace the core and resist rotation.
Lower the dumbbell out to the side in a fly arc.
Pull the dumbbell back over the chest using the pec.
Continue for all reps then switch sides.
Isolates one side of the chest.
Trains anti-rotation core.
Ball adds instability.
Builds the chest.
Useful unilateral accessory.

description.en: The dumbbell one-arm lateral raise isolates a single side deltoid by performing lateral raises with one arm at a time. The unilateral approach allows greater focus on each side and can be performed leaning away from the cable for additional stretch at the bottom.

en: Stand tall. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand at your side.
Use your left hand to hold a rack or wall for stability (optional).
Raise the dumbbell out to the side by lifting your right arm.
Lift until your arm is parallel to the floor or slightly higher.
Maintain slight elbow bend throughout.
Squeeze your lateral delt at the top.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch arms. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Unilateral focus on one side delt at a time
Exposes left-right delt imbalances
Can lean away from support for added stretch
Simple isolation exercise
Easy to progress
Builds shoulder width

description.en: The dumbbell press on an exercise ball replaces the flat bench with a stability ball. Your upper back rests on the ball while feet support your body on the floor. The unstable surface adds significant core, glute, and shoulder stabilizer demand to the standard dumbbell press.

en: Sit on a stability ball holding dumbbells at your thighs. Walk your feet forward and roll down until your upper back rests on the ball.
Bridge your hips up so your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Bring the dumbbells to your shoulders, palms forward.
Press both dumbbells up to lockout above your chest.
Lower under control to your chest.
Maintain the bridge throughout. Keep the ball stable.
Use lighter weight than flat bench dumbbell press.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Adds core and stabilizer demand to DB press
Builds glute endurance from the bridge
Challenges shoulder stabilizers
Useful variation for stability training
Engages the full body
No bench needed

description.en: The dumbbell prone full can exercise is performed face down on an incline bench with light dumbbells held thumbs up. The arms raise up and out at a 45 degree angle to form a Y. The thumbs up position targets the supraspinatus and lower trapezius for shoulder health.

en: Set an incline bench at about 30 degrees.
Lie face down on the bench with light dumbbells in each hand.
Let your arms hang straight down with palms facing forward, thumbs up.
Brace your core and keep your head neutral.
Raise the dumbbells up and out at a 45 degree angle to form a Y.
Lift until the arms are in line with your ears.
Pause and squeeze the lower trap.
Lower the dumbbells with control to the start.
Strengthens the rotator cuff
Targets the lower trapezius
Improves shoulder health
Useful prehab work
Bench supports the torso
Light load is plenty

description.en: The dumbbell pullover hip extension on exercise ball combines a pullover with a glute bridge on a stability ball. The lifter lies on the ball, performs a pullover, and drops the hips to add a hip extension. The combo trains the lats, glutes, and core in a brutal full body move.

en: Sit on a stability ball and walk the feet out so the upper back rests on the ball.
Hold a dumbbell vertically with both hands cupped under the top plate.
Press the dumbbell up over the chest.
Drop the hips down toward the floor.
Lower the dumbbell back overhead with arms slightly bent.
Drive the hips up into a glute bridge as you pull the dumbbell back over the chest.
Squeeze the lats and glutes at the top.
Lower the hips and dumbbell together for the next rep.
Brutal full body builder
Strong lat builder
Trains the glutes
Adds core challenge
Strong dumbbell move
Useful functional pattern

description.en: The dumbbell seated reverse grip concentration curl uses a pronated (palm down) grip during the concentration curl. The reverse grip shifts emphasis from the bicep peak to the brachialis and brachioradialis, the muscles underneath the bicep and on the upper forearm. It is a strong choice for arm thickness.

en: Sit on the end of a flat bench with feet wide on the floor.
Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand with palm facing down.
Lean forward and rest your right elbow on your inner thigh.
Allow the dumbbell to hang at full arm extension.
Brace your core and keep your back straight.
Curl the dumbbell up using a reverse grip throughout.
Squeeze the brachialis at the top.
Lower the dumbbell back down with control. Switch arms.
Targets brachialis and brachioradialis
Builds arm thickness
Strict isolation pattern
Different stimulus than supinated curls
Strong forearm involvement
Useful for arm specialization

description.en: The dumbbell step-up is a single-leg compound exercise where you step up onto a box or bench with a dumbbell in each hand. The exercise builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings unilaterally while training balance, ankle stability, and core control. Box height controls the difficulty — higher boxes increase glute demand and overall difficulty.

en: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench, roughly knee-height. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Plant your right foot fully on top of the box. Make sure your entire foot is on the surface.
Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your chest tall.
Drive through your right foot — pushing through the entire foot, especially the heel — to lift your body up onto the box.
Stand fully tall on top of the box with both feet planted. Squeeze your right glute hard.
Step the left foot back down to the floor under control. Keep most of your weight on the right leg the entire time.
Once your left foot is back on the floor, follow with your right foot. That is one rep.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch. Resist pushing off the back leg — the work should come from the working leg only.
Builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings one leg at a time
Trains balance, ankle stability, and core control
Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances
Adjustable difficulty by changing box height
Excellent carryover to climbing, hiking, and athletic movements
Lower spinal load than back squats

description.en: The dumbbell upright row is a vertical pulling exercise where you hold a dumbbell in each hand and pull them up the front of your body by driving your elbows up. The independent dumbbells allow a more natural pull path than the barbell version, with the dumbbells able to drift slightly outward — making it more shoulder-friendly.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs with palms facing your body.
Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your chest tall.
Pull both dumbbells up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out to the sides. Let the dumbbells drift slightly outward as they rise.
Lead with your elbows, not your hands. Keep the dumbbells close to your body but not pressed against it.
Continue pulling until the dumbbells reach roughly chest height. Your elbows should be at or slightly above shoulder height.
Do not pull higher than chest level — going higher can impinge the shoulder.
Pause briefly at the top, then lower the dumbbells under control back to the starting position.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight and focus on form.
Trains the lateral delts and upper traps together
More shoulder-friendly pull path than barbell upright rows
Independent dumbbells expose left-right imbalances
Builds shoulder width and trap thickness
Easier to do at home with just dumbbells
Trains grip and forearm strength as a byproduct

description.en: The dumbbell waiter biceps curl is performed by holding a single dumbbell horizontally with both hands cupping the head of the dumbbell, palms up. The waiter-tray grip locks the wrists and forces the biceps to do all the lifting work. It is one of the strictest curl variations.

en: Hold a single dumbbell vertically with both hands cupping the bottom plate, palms facing up.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold the dumbbell in front of your thighs with arms extended.
Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides.
Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbows.
Keep your wrists in the same waiter-tray position throughout.
Squeeze your biceps at the top with the dumbbell near your chest.
Lower the dumbbell back down with control to full extension.
Strict bicep isolation
Locks the wrists in a fixed position
Both hands work together for stability
Eliminates wrist cheating
Builds bicep strength and size
Useful for breaking through curl plateaus

description.en: The front plank side hop is a dynamic plank variation that adds a side-to-side hop. The lifter holds a high plank and hops the feet together side to side. The hop loads the obliques and adds a cardio component to the standard plank.

en: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core hard and keep the hips level.
Hop both feet to one side together.
Land softly with the feet still together.
Hop both feet back through center to the other side.
Continue the side-to-side hopping motion at speed.
Keep the upper body steady throughout.
Strong oblique builder
Adds cardio to plank
Trains the hip flexors
No equipment needed
Useful core finisher
Builds shoulder stability

description.en: Garland Pose (Malasana) is a deep yoga squat where you sit at the bottom of a wide squat with your elbows pressing against your inner knees. It deeply opens the hips, ankles, groin, and lower back. Many cultures sit in this position naturally for daily activities.

en: Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees.
Squat down as low as possible. Keep your heels flat on the floor if you can.
Bring your hands together at your heart in prayer position. Place your elbows against your inner knees.
Press your elbows out against your knees, gently spreading them open.
Sit up tall through your spine. Lift your chest.
If your heels lift, place a folded blanket or yoga block under them.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply into your belly.
To exit, place your hands on the floor and slowly straighten your legs.
Deeply opens the hips, groin, and ankles
Strengthens the legs and core
Improves squat mobility
Relieves lower-back tension
Aids digestion through compression
Foundational deep-squat position

description.en: The hangboard slope hang is a climbing-specific grip exercise where the lifter hangs from a sloping hold on a hangboard. The slope forces an open hand grip and builds friction grip strength. The hold develops finger and forearm endurance for climbers.

en: Stand below a hangboard with sloping holds.
Reach up and place the fingers on the slope.
Set the fingers flat with an open hand grip.
Engage your shoulders and pull them down.
Lift your feet off the ground to hang from the slope.
Press the fingers into the slope to hold the grip.
Keep the body steady and avoid swinging.
Lower your feet back down with control.
Builds friction grip
Trains open hand strength
Useful for climbers
Strong forearm builder
Develops grip endurance
Climbing-specific work

description.en: The heel press is a calf and plantar fascia mobility drill where you place the ball of your foot on the edge of a step and press your heel down below the step level. The dorsiflexion stretch targets the gastrocnemius, soleus, Achilles, and plantar fascia in one drill.

en: Stand at the edge of a step or platform. Place the balls of both feet on the step with your heels hanging off the back.
Hold a railing or wall for balance.
Slowly lower your heels down below the level of the step as far as comfortable.
Feel the deep stretch through your calves, Achilles tendons, and plantar fascia.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Press through the balls of your feet to return to neutral.
Repeat 2 to 3 times.
For single-leg version: stand on one foot at a time for a deeper stretch.
Stretches the entire calf complex (gastroc and soleus)
Opens the Achilles tendon
Stretches the plantar fascia
Improves ankle dorsiflexion
Critical for runners and lifters with tight calves
Helps prevent plantar fasciitis

description.en: The kettlebell one arm military press to the side is a unilateral shoulder press where the kettlebell is pressed out to the side rather than overhead. The angle hammers the lateral and front deltoids.

en: Stand tall with feet hip width apart and a kettlebell in the rack position on one side.
Brace the core and keep the chest tall.
Press the kettlebell out to the side at a slight upward angle.
Aim for the arm to finish at about 45 degrees up and to the side.
Keep the wrist neutral and the bell stable through the press.
Pause briefly at full extension.
Lower the kettlebell back to the rack with full control.
Complete all reps on one side then switch arms.
Hits the side and front deltoids from an unusual angle.
Builds shoulder strength with reduced overhead stress.
Trains the core to resist the offset pressing load.
Single arm work exposes imbalances.
Joint friendly for those with overhead press limitations.
Develops shoulder stability and control.

description.en: The kettlebell press-up is a push-up performed gripping the handles of two kettlebells placed on the floor at shoulder width. The unstable kettlebell base demands extra stabilizer engagement and grip strength. The deeper hand position also allows greater range of motion than a floor push-up.

en: Place two kettlebells on the floor at slightly wider than shoulder width.
Grip the handles firmly. Get into a high-plank position with your hands on the kettlebells.
Brace your core. Form a straight body line from heels to head.
Lower your chest between the kettlebells. The deeper hand position allows extra range.
Lower until your chest is below the kettlebell handles.
Press back up to lockout, squeezing your chest and triceps.
Maintain control of the kettlebells throughout — they want to wobble.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Greater range of motion than floor push-ups
Demands extra stabilizer engagement
Builds grip strength simultaneously
Wrist-friendly neutral grip
Trains the chest and triceps with deeper stretch
Works at home with two kettlebells

description.en: The lying alternate toe touch on the floor is a bodyweight ab move. Lying on the back, you raise opposite arm and leg to meet at the top, alternating sides for a crossing crunch pattern.

en: Lie flat on your back with arms and legs extended.
Brace the core and press the lower back to the floor.
Lift one leg and the opposite arm at the same time.
Reach the hand toward the lifted foot at the top of the rep.
Squeeze the abs and obliques.
Lower the arm and leg back to the floor with control.
Repeat on the other side.
Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.
Trains the abs and obliques with a crossing pattern.
Builds rotational core strength.
No equipment needed.
Easy to scale by adjusting reach height.
Carryover to athletic rotation.
Develops mind muscle connection through the core.

description.en: The lever reverse grip vertical row is performed on a vertical chest-supported row machine with the palms facing up in an underhand grip. The reverse grip biases the lower lats and biceps over the upper back. It is a strong row variation for arm and lat detail.

en: Set up the vertical row machine with chest pad and foot platform in place.
Stand with chest against the pad and feet on the platform.
Grip the handles with palms facing up.
Let your arms hang straight down with shoulder blades retracted.
Brace your core and pin your chest to the pad.
Row the handles up toward your sides.
Squeeze the lats and biceps at the top of the row.
Lower with control until arms are straight again.
Biases lower lats and biceps
Chest-supported strict form
Builds back thickness
Easy to load heavy
Excellent back day move
Wrist-friendly grip

description.en: The mountain climber is a dynamic plank-based exercise where you alternately drive your knees toward your chest at speed. It elevates the heart rate quickly while heavily training the core, hip flexors, and shoulder stabilizers. Used in HIIT workouts, warm-ups, and metabolic conditioning circuits, the mountain climber delivers a lot of work in a short time.

en: Start in a high plank position with your hands directly under your shoulders and your body forming a straight line from head to heels.
Engage your core and squeeze your glutes. Your hips should stay level throughout the entire movement, not bouncing up and down.
Drive your right knee toward your chest, keeping your foot off the ground.
Quickly switch legs: extend the right leg back to the plank position while pulling your left knee toward your chest.
Continue alternating legs as quickly as you can while maintaining a flat back and stable shoulders.
Breathe rhythmically, exhaling on each knee drive. Avoid letting your hips pike up or sag down.
Work in intervals: 20 to 40 seconds of fast climbers followed by 10 to 30 seconds of rest, for several rounds.
Elevates the heart rate quickly for cardiovascular conditioning
Trains the core (especially anti-rotation and anti-extension) under fatigue
Builds endurance in the hip flexors and shoulder stabilizers
Requires no equipment and minimal space
Doubles as a dynamic warm-up before lifting or sport
Easily scaled by changing speed or adding variations

description.en: The resistance band external rotation is a rotator cuff strengthening exercise where you anchor a band at elbow height and rotate your forearm outward away from your body while keeping your elbow tucked at your side. It targets the infraspinatus and teres minor — key muscles for shoulder health and stability.

en: Anchor a resistance band to a sturdy point at elbow height.
Stand sideways to the anchor with the band on your right side.
Grip the band with your right hand. Pin your right elbow against your right side, bent at 90 degrees.
Step away from the anchor until the band is under tension. Forearm starts pointing across your body.
Brace your core. Keep your right elbow pinned to your side.
Rotate your forearm outward away from your body, pulling the band.
Continue until your forearm is pointing forward (or as far as comfortable).
Slowly return to start. Use light resistance — this is a rotator cuff exercise, not a power lift.
Strengthens the rotator cuff
Improves shoulder stability
Helps prevent shoulder impingement
Useful for athletes and lifters
Highly portable
Joint-friendly

description.en: The resistance band seated chest press is performed seated on a bench or chair with a resistance band anchored behind you. Both handles press straight forward in a chest press pattern. The seated position adds back support and forces strict pressing form. It is a great home chest builder.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height behind you.
Sit on a bench or chair facing away from the anchor.
Hold a handle in each hand at chest level.
Position yourself far enough to add tension to the band.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Press both handles straight forward to full extension.
Squeeze the chest at full extension.
Bring the handles slowly back to chest level.
Strict chest pressing form
No bench press required
Easy to set up at home
Joint-friendly variation
Builds chest strength
Increasing tension at lockout

description.en: The roll ball forearm extensors is a self myofascial release drill for the back of the forearm. Pressing a ball into the extensors releases knots from heavy gripping, curling, and computer work.

en: Sit at a table with one forearm resting on top.
Place a massage ball under the back of the forearm.
Press the forearm down into the ball.
Use the other hand to add pressure.
Roll the back of the forearm slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover from elbow to wrist.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the wrist extensors.
Reduces forearm tightness.
Improves grip recovery.
Useful for climbers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll ball rectus femoris is a self myofascial release drill for the front quad. The rectus femoris crosses both the hip and knee, and releasing it improves both hip extension and knee flexion mobility.

en: Lie face down on the floor.
Place a massage ball under the front of one thigh.
Brace the body on the forearms.
Keep the working leg relaxed.
Roll the front of the thigh slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover from hip to just above the knee.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the front quad.
Improves hip extension.
Improves knee flexion.
Useful for runners.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll iliopsoas uses a foam roller or massage ball to release tension in the iliopsoas, the deep hip flexor muscle. Lying face down with the roller positioned just inside the hip bone, you slowly roll over the muscle to release tightness. It is a strong recovery and mobility drill for runners, lifters, and desk workers.

en: Place a small foam roller or massage ball on the floor.
Lie face down with the roller just inside your right hip bone.
Position the roller below the rib cage and to the inside of the hip.
Support yourself on your forearms.
Brace your core and breathe slowly.
Slowly shift your weight onto the roller in this position.
Allow the roller to sink into the iliopsoas tissue.
Hold tender spots for 20 to 30 seconds. Switch sides.
Releases hip flexor tension
Improves hip mobility
Useful for desk worker tightness
Helps with lower back tension
Recovery drill for lifters and runners
Easy to do at home

description.en: The lever seated reverse fly uses a pec deck or reverse fly machine to isolate the rear deltoids. You sit facing the pad and pull the handles apart behind you in a fly motion. The machine guides the arc and provides constant resistance throughout.

en: Sit facing the pad on a pec deck or reverse fly machine. Adjust the handles so they are in front of you at shoulder height.
Grip the handles with a neutral or overhand grip. Arms extended forward.
Pull the handles apart and behind you in a wide arc, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Continue until your arms are out to your sides or slightly behind your body.
Squeeze your rear delts and rhomboids hard at the end position.
Slowly return the handles to the starting position under control.
Do not let the weight stack rest between reps.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Machine-guided rear delt isolation
Constant resistance throughout the arc
Easy to load progressively
Builds shoulder balance and posture
Simple execution
Excellent for rear delt hypertrophy

description.en: The seated row with towel is a creative bodyweight back exercise. The lifter sits on the floor with the legs extended and loops a towel around the feet. Pulling on the towel ends performs a self-resisted seated row that loads the upper back.

en: Sit on the floor with the legs extended forward.
Loop a sturdy towel around the soles of both feet.
Grab one end of the towel in each hand.
Brace your core and sit tall with chest up.
Pull the towel ends back to row toward your stomach.
Squeeze the upper back hard at the top.
Press the feet against the towel to create resistance.
Lower the towel back forward with control.
Creative bodyweight back move
No machine needed
Builds upper back strength
Useful at home
Easy to scale resistance
Strong basic row

description.en: The shoulder bridge is a Pilates-style bridge exercise where you roll your spine up off the floor one vertebra at a time, holding at the top, then rolling back down sequentially. It builds glute strength while improving spinal articulation and mobility. It is gentler and more controlled than a fast-tempo glute bridge.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Arms at your sides.
Inhale to prepare. Exhale and begin rolling your hips up off the floor, peeling one vertebra at a time from the floor.
Continue rolling until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Hold for two to three breaths. Keep your ribs connected to your pelvis — do not arch the lower back.
Inhale. Exhale and slowly roll your spine back down, one vertebra at a time, from the upper back to the tailbone.
The sequential rolling is the key feature — think of your spine as a string of pearls lifting and lowering one at a time.
Repeat for 5 to 10 reps.
For more challenge: extend one leg at the top and hold for 3 breaths, then switch.
Improves spinal articulation and mobility
Builds the glutes and hamstrings
Stretches the hip flexors and chest at the top
Teaches controlled, sequential spinal movement
Gentle and restorative — suitable for all levels
Foundational Pilates exercise

description.en: The single leg jumping glute bridge is an explosive single leg bridge variation. From a single leg bridge position, you drive the hips up powerfully so the foot leaves the ground momentarily.

en: Lie on your back with one knee bent and the foot flat on the floor.
Extend the other leg straight out.
Place the arms at your sides for support.
Brace the core and squeeze the glute on the working side.
Drive the hips up powerfully through the planted heel.
Allow the planted foot to leave the floor at the top of the bridge.
Land softly back into the bridge position.
Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Builds explosive glute power.
Single leg setup trains unilateral strength.
No equipment needed.
Carryover to sprinting and jumping.
Improves hip extension force.
Develops total posterior chain strength.

description.en: The stick side to front bend stretch is a mobility drill done with a PVC pipe or stick held overhead. Bending to one side then folding forward stretches the obliques, lats, and lower back through a long range.

en: Stand tall with the feet shoulder width apart.
Hold a stick overhead with both hands wider than shoulders.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Bend slowly to one side from the waist.
Continue the bend forward into a fold.
Bring the stick toward the floor.
Reverse back through the side bend.
Return to center and switch sides.
Stretches the obliques.
Opens the lats.
Mobilizes the lower back.
Useful warm-up.
Improves rotational mobility.

description.en: The suspended reverse crunch (TRX knee tuck) is a core exercise where you hold a plank with feet in TRX straps and tuck your knees toward your chest. The suspended position dramatically increases core demand compared to floor reverse crunches.

en: Set TRX straps to mid-calf height. Get into a high plank with feet in the foot cradles.
Body in a straight line from heels to head. Arms extended, hands under shoulders.
Brace your core hard.
Tuck both knees toward your chest by curling your hips up and bringing knees forward.
Squeeze your abs at the peak of the tuck.
Slowly extend your legs back to the plank position.
Maintain the plank throughout — do not let your hips sag.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Heavy core demand from suspended position
Targets the lower abs and hip flexors
Builds shoulder stability
No floor equipment needed besides TRX
Scalable by adjusting tempo or adding reps
Excellent core finisher

description.en: The suspender triceps extension uses a TRX or suspension trainer for an overhead-style triceps extension. With the body angled forward and the elbows held high, the triceps extend to push the body upright. It is a great bodyweight triceps builder that trains the long head through a stretched position.

en: Set the suspension trainer with handles at about head height.
Face away from the anchor and grab both handles.
Walk your feet back so your body angles forward at the handles.
Bring your hands behind your head with elbows bent and pointed forward.
Brace your core and keep your body straight.
Extend the elbows to push your body upright.
Squeeze the triceps hard at full extension.
Bend the elbows to lower with control.
Trains the triceps long head
Bodyweight triceps builder
Adjustable difficulty via foot position
No weights required
Useful for home training
Strong stretch on the triceps

description.en: The suspension trainer triceps kickback is a bodyweight tricep kickback performed on TRX straps. The lifter grips the handles and from a hinged forward lean extends the elbows back behind the body. The strap angle controls the load and builds tricep size.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles with palms facing down.
Lean forward into the straps with arms bent.
Set the elbows up at shoulder height behind you.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Extend the elbows to push the body away from the anchor.
Lock out the elbows and squeeze the triceps hard.
Bend the elbows back to the start with control.
Bodyweight tricep builder
No dumbbells needed
Trains the long head
Strong arm move
Useful TRX move
Easy to scale by angle
